rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods, Field Experiments <U+2013> two-season field experiment (2017, 2018) on calcareous sandy soil at Sohag, Egypt, split-plot design with four replications testing P fertigation frequency and P form under drip irrigation.
rows.notes: All treatments were drip-irrigated with identical daily water amounts; the study varies only P fertigation frequency (daily, 2-day, 3-day) and P form (urea phosphate vs monopotassium phosphate). It never compares drip with any other irrigation method, does not measure water distribution uniformity, waterlogging, dry patches or plant stress, and makes no claim of its own about drip preventing these. What it shows is that daily urea-phosphate fertigation raised soil P availability, petiole P, tuber yield (about 10% marketable yield gain for daily vs less frequent application; UP 22% over MPP every 3 days), PUE and WUE (Tables 4-6). Statements about drip increasing WUE/yield in sandy soils are in the Introduction and cite other work (Iqbal et al. 2003; Badr et al. 2010, 2012). Drip is the background system, not the tested technology, so the study gives no own evidence on the claimed effect of drip.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods, Field Experiments <U+2013> own two-season field trial with measured soil pH, available P, petiole P, tuber yield, PUE and WUE under drip-fertigation treatments.
rows.notes: No result on risk reduction (plant stress, waterlogging, dry patches, yield-loss risk) from drip irrigation. Drip was applied uniformly to every treatment and no alternative irrigation method was tested, so the study cannot show that drip reduces the risk of stress or yield reduction relative to other methods. Its own findings concern the effect of P fertigation frequency and fertiliser form on yield and nutrient/water use efficiency (Tables 5-6). The sentence in the Introduction about potato being sensitive to over- and under-irrigation is cited from Stark et al. (2004), not an own result.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a primary field experiment on P fertigation (frequency and form) for drip-irrigated potato; drip irrigation is the common background for all treatments and is not itself evaluated against other irrigation methods, so it provides no own evidence for the review's claims about drip delivering uniform water distribution, preventing waterlogging/dry patches or reducing plant-stress and yield-loss risk.
